LECTURE 4Cranial Nerves — Overview

Lecturer: Dr Nur Hassan, BDS, PGT (Oral Surg), PhD.

  • 12 pairs; numbered by Roman numerals in a rostral → caudal direction.
  • Branch from the brain (CN I & II) and the brainstem (CN III–XII).
  • Can carry sensory (incl. special sense), motor, or both kinds of fibres.

The twelve nerves

I OlfactoryII OpticIII Oculomotor IV TrochlearV TrigeminalVI Abducens VII FacialVIII VestibulocochlearIX Glossopharyngeal X VagusXI AccessoryXII Hypoglossal

Brainstem attachments

  • CN I & II — direct outgrowths of the brain
  • CN III — midbrain (interpeduncular fossa)
  • CN IV — dorsal aspect of the brainstem (only nerve to exit dorsally)
  • CN V — lateral pons
  • CN VI, VII, VIII — pontomedullary junction
  • CN IX, X, XI — medulla, lateral to the olive
  • CN XII — medulla, medial to the olive (between olive and pyramid)

Ganglia & nuclei

Cranial nerve ganglia (cell bodies)

  • Sensory ganglia — cell bodies of primary sensory neurons (no synapses)
  • Autonomic ganglia — cell bodies of postganglionic neurons (synapses)
  • No mixed ganglia — either sensory or autonomic

Cranial nerve nuclei

  • Motor nuclei = cell bodies of lower motor neurons
  • Sensory nuclei = cell bodies of secondary sensory neurons

4 parasympathetic ganglia of the head: ciliary (III), pterygopalatine (VII), submandibular (VII), otic (IX).

Cavernous sinus contents

  • Lateral wall: CN III, IV, V₁, V₂
  • Passing through: CN VI and the internal carotid artery
  • Clinical: cavernous sinus thrombosis affects III, IV, VI, V1 & V2; abducent (VI) is most vulnerable. Loss of synchronised eye movement → diplopia.

CN VTrigeminal Nerve

  • Sensation from: face, anterior scalp, oral cavity, nasal cavity, teeth, meninges.
  • Motor to 8 muscles derived from the 1st branchial arch (muscles of mastication + tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric).
  • Three divisions: ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), mandibular (V3).

Trigeminal nuclei

NucleusModality
Mesencephalic nucleusProprioception
Principal (pontine) sensory nucleusTouch
Spinal nucleusPain and temperature
Motor nucleusTo the eight 1st-arch muscles

Ophthalmic (V1) — via superior orbital fissure

  • Frontal n. (→ supraorbital + supratrochlear) — sensory to upper eyelid skin & conjunctiva, forehead skin, frontal sinus mucosa.
  • Lacrimal n. — sensory to upper eyelid; distributes postganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion (PPG) to the lacrimal gland.
  • Nasociliary n. — sensory to ethmoid & sphenoid sinuses, anterior nasal cavity, nose, eye & lacrimal sac; carries sympathetic fibres from the SCG to ciliaris & dilator pupillae.
  • Recurrent meningeal branch — sensory to dura of the middle cranial fossa.

Maxillary (V2) — via foramen rotundum

  • Infraorbital n. (via inferior orbital fissure), zygomatic n. (conveys parasympathetic from PPG to lacrimal gland).
  • Superior alveolar nerves (ASA, MSA, PSA) → maxillary teeth & gingiva.
  • Greater & lesser palatine nerves, nasopalatine n., posterior superior nasal nerves → palate & nasal septum.
  • Middle meningeal n. — sensory to meninges of the middle cranial fossa.

Mandibular (V3) — via foramen ovale

Sensory branches

  • Auriculotemporal n. — skin of temple; carries parasympathetic from the otic ganglion (from CN IX) to the parotid gland.
  • Buccal (long buccal) n. — buccal gingiva adjacent to molars.
  • Lingual n. — mandibular lingual gingiva, floor of mouth, anterior 2/3 tongue; carries taste from CN VII (chorda tympani).
  • Inferior alveolar n. — mandibular teeth → continues as the mental n. (chin & lower lip).

Motor branches (to 1st-arch muscles)

  • Masseteric n.
  • Deep temporal nerves
  • Nerve to lateral pterygoid
  • Nerve to medial pterygoid (+ tensor tympani & tensor veli palatini)
  • Nerve to mylohyoid (+ anterior belly of digastric)

Clinical testing (V)

  • V1: corneal reflex; skin sensation of forehead & anterior scalp.
  • V2: skin sensation of lower eyelid, cheek & upper lip.
  • V3: sensation of chin & lower lip; motor — open/close jaw against resistance; jaw reflex.

CN VIIFacial Nerve

  • Motor to the muscles of facial expression (2nd branchial arch).
  • Taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue & oral cavity (via chorda tympani).
  • Parasympathetic secretomotor to the salivary (submandibular & sublingual), lacrimal, nasal & palatine glands — i.e. all head glands except the parotid.

Facial nerve nuclei

NucleusFunction
Facial motor nucleusMotor
Superior salivatory nucleusParasympathetic
Nucleus of the solitary tractTaste
Sensory nuclei of trigeminalTactile sensory

Course (5 steps)

  • 1 — exits the skull’s interior via the internal acoustic meatus
  • 2 — greater petrosal branch travels in the greater petrosal canal (→ lacrimal/nasal/palatine glands via PPG)
  • 3 & 4 — travels in the facial canal in the medial wall of the tympanic cavity; gives nerve to stapedius & chorda tympani
  • 5 — exits via the stylomastoid foramen → posterior auricular n., nerve to stylohyoid & posterior digastric → branches to the muscles of facial expression

Terminal (parotid) branches

“Ten Zebras Bit My Cheek”
TemporalZygomaticBuccal Marginal mandibularCervical

Facial paralysis (clinical)

  • Central (UMN) paralysis — spares the forehead (upper face has bilateral cortical innervation).
  • Peripheral (LMN) paralysis — affects the whole half of the face (e.g. Bell’s palsy).
  • Testing: raise eyebrows, force apart closed eyelids, puff out cheeks, corneal reflex.

SPECIAL & EYECN I, II, III, IV, VI & VIII

Olfactory (CN I) — via cribriform plate

  • Special sense of smell. Bipolar neurons in the olfactory epithelium (superior concha & adjacent septum).
  • Central processes pierce the cribriform plate of the ethmoid and synapse on mitral cells in the olfactory bulb.

Optic (CN II) — via optic canal

  • Special sense of vision; an outgrowth of the brain (like CN I).
  • Retina: rods & cones → bipolar cells (primary) → ganglion cells (secondary), whose axons form the optic nerve.
  • Lesions: at the optic nerve → blindness in one eye; at the optic chiasma → visual field loss depending on the part compressed.

Extra-ocular nerves — CN III, IV, VI

NerveOriginMotor supply
III OculomotorMidbrainLPS, SR (sup. division); MR, IR, IO (inf. division); parasympathetic (Edinger–Westphal → ciliary ganglion) to sphincter pupillae & ciliaris
IV TrochlearDorsal midbrainSuperior oblique (enters outside the common tendinous ring)
VI AbducensPontomedullary junctionLateral rectus

All three travel through the cavernous sinus and exit via the superior orbital fissure; all receive bilateral cortical innervation.

Clinical: cavernous sinus thrombosis (sometimes from spread of dental infection) affects III, IV, VI, V1 & V2. The abducent is most likely affected → lateral rectus palsy, medially rotated eye; loss of synchronised movement → diplopia.

Vestibulocochlear (CN VIII) — via internal acoustic meatus

  • Special senses of hearing and balance.
  • Two parts: vestibular (balance) and cochlear (hearing).

CN IX–XIILower Cranial Nerves

Glossopharyngeal (CN IX) — via jugular foramen

  • Sensory to the oropharynx; sensory & taste to the posterior 1/3 of the tongue.
  • Parasympathetic to the parotid gland (via lesser petrosal n. → otic ganglion).
  • Motor to stylopharyngeus (muscular branch).
  • Branches: lingual, tonsillar, tympanic, muscular, pharyngeal, carotid (carotid body chemoreceptors & sinus baroreceptors).
  • Nuclei: nucleus ambiguus (motor), inferior salivatory (parasympathetic), solitary tract (sensory/taste), spinal nucleus of V (sensory).
  • Clinical: the afferent limb of the gag reflex.

Vagus (CN X) — via jugular foramen

  • Functions: phonation, swallowing; sensory to external ear, carotid body & larynx; parasympathetic to thoracic & abdominal viscera; dura of the posterior fossa.
  • Motor fibres (from the cranial part of CN XI, distributed by vagus) supply most soft-palate muscles (except tensor veli palatini), pharynx (except stylopharyngeus) & the laryngeal muscles.
  • Key branches: pharyngeal, superior laryngeal (internal = sensory above the cords; external = motor to cricothyroid), recurrent laryngeal (sensory below the cords; motor to all laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid), auricular, carotid, visceral.
  • Clinical: efferent limb of the gag reflex; vagal reflexes — coughing, vomiting, fainting (reflex bradycardia). Test: speech, palate deviation, gag reflex.

Accessory (CN XI) — via jugular foramen

  • Spinal part ascends through the foramen magnum, then exits via the jugular foramen.
  • Supplies two neck muscles: sternocleidomastoid & trapezius.
  • Cranial accessory travels with the vagus (functionally indistinguishable).
  • Testing: shoulder shrug against resistance (trapezius); head rotation against resistance (SCM).

Hypoglossal (CN XII) — via hypoglossal canal

  • Motor to all the “glossus” tongue muscles except palatoglossus (which is vagus) — styloglossus, hyoglossus, genioglossus & the intrinsic tongue muscles.
  • Also geniohyoid & thyrohyoid (via C1 fibres running with it).
  • Clinical: a hypoglossal lesion causes the tongue to deviate towards the side of the lesion on protrusion.
